introduction-the-battle-for-focus.core: Engineering needs deep, uninterrupted focus to load complex problems into your head. Every interruption costs about 20+ minutes to rebuild context, so fragmented days produce shallow work.

first_principles.problem: An engineer has six meetings scattered across the day and never gets the two-hour block needed to fix a hard bug.
truths: Context switching has a high cost.

analogy.title: Loading a game level
analogy.story: Every interruption sends you back to the loading screen, so you spend more time loading than playing.
analogy.breaks: Some interruptions are the job (incidents, unblocking others), so manage them rather than eliminate them.

example.title: A fragmented vs a defragmented day

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The same hours give far more output.

check.q: Why are scattered meetings so costly for engineers?
check.a: Each interruption costs significant time to rebuild context, leaving no long blocks for deep work.

makers-schedule-vs-managers-schedule.core: Paul Graham: managers work in hour slots where meetings are just tasks, while makers need half-day blocks where one meeting can destroy the whole afternoon. Senior engineers often live on both schedules and have to separate them deliberately.

first_principles.problem: A manager schedules a 30-minute meeting at 2:30 PM, ruining an engineer's whole afternoon of building.
truths: Different work has different time grains.
Makers' costs are invisible to managers.
derivation: Recognise **which schedule** each person and task needs.

analogy.title: A writer vs. a receptionist
analogy.story: A receptionist handles visitors all day; interrupting a novelist mid-chapter costs the whole session.
analogy.breaks: Leads need both, so the skill is deliberate separation, not avoidance.

check.q: Why can one meeting ruin a maker's afternoon?
check.a: Makers need long uninterrupted blocks, and a meeting in the middle splits them into fragments too short for deep work.

deep-work-the-superpower-of-the-21st-cen.core: Cal Newport's deep work is distraction-free focus on cognitively demanding tasks. It creates most of the value and is increasingly rare. Shallow work (email, chat) is easy to replicate. Schedule deep work deliberately and remove distractions.

first_principles.problem: Constant Slack and email keep engineers busy but stop them producing the hard, valuable work.
truths: Distractions are engineered to grab attention.
derivation: **Ritualise** it: same place, same time, a clear goal.

analogy.title: A craftsman's workshop with the door closed
analogy.story: Fine work happens when nobody's popping in every few minutes.
analogy.breaks: Teams still need responsiveness, so agree on response-time norms rather than going dark.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Hard tasks finished in days instead of weeks.

check.q: What distinguishes deep work from shallow work?
check.a: Deep work is distraction-free focus on demanding tasks; shallow work is logistical and easily interrupted or replicated.

the-pomodoro-technique-beating-procrasti.core: The Pomodoro Technique works in 25-minute focused sprints followed by 5-minute breaks, with a longer break after four. It lowers the barrier to starting daunting tasks and builds a rhythm of focus.

first_principles.problem: Self-interruption (procrastination, 'just checking') stops engineers starting or sustaining hard tasks.
derivation: Set a **25-minute timer** and work only on it.
Take a **5-minute break**; after 4 rounds, a 15–30 minute break.

analogy.title: Interval training for the mind
analogy.story: Short, intense intervals with rest beat trying to run flat out for hours.
analogy.breaks: 25 minutes can be too short for deep coding flow, so adapt the length (e.g. 50/10).

example.title: Tackling a dreaded refactor
flow: Done in 2 hours after weeks of avoidance

check.q: What main problem does the Pomodoro Technique address?
check.a: Procrastination and self-interruption, by making focused work start in small committed intervals.

fixing-calendar-fragmentation-defragment.core: Senior engineers attract meetings. Defragment by batching meetings into blocks, declining or delegating low-value ones, shortening defaults (25 and 50 minutes), putting focus blocks on the calendar, and preferring async updates.

first_principles.problem: The calendar is Swiss cheese: a 30-minute gap here and there, never two hours free.

analogy.title: Defragmenting a hard drive
analogy.story: Moving scattered pieces together frees large contiguous blocks.
analogy.breaks: Declining too much can damage relationships, so explain and offer alternatives.

check.q: Name two tactics for defragmenting a calendar.
check.a: For example, batching meetings into set windows and replacing status meetings with async updates (plus declining or delegating).

the-energy-dimension-managing-cognitive-.core: Time management also means energy management. Schedule the hardest cognitive work (design, debugging) at your personal peak, and lighter work (email, reviews, admin) in troughs. Protect sleep, take breaks and limit decision fatigue.

first_principles.problem: Engineers spend their sharpest morning hours on email and tackle complex design exhausted at 5 PM.
truths: Cognitive energy varies through the day.
derivation: **Recover**: breaks, movement, sleep; reduce trivial decisions.

analogy.title: An athlete's training schedule
analogy.story: Intense sessions when fresh, recovery and light work afterwards.
analogy.breaks: Team schedules constrain flexibility, so negotiate core hours.

check.q: Why schedule complex design work during peak energy hours?
check.a: Demanding cognitive tasks need the most mental energy, and fatigue degrades judgement and quality.
